blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: We present a controlled, large-scale evaluation of how corpus scale, document representation, and reranking affect the effectiveness and efficiency of biomedical Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems. Retrieval collections were progressively expanded while retaining the relevant source documents, enabling consistent comparisons across corpus sizes. We compared abstract, flat full-text, and hierarchical full-text representations across first-stage retrieval, reranking, and end-to-end multiple-choice question answering. Configurations selected on development data were evaluated on five external biomedical benchmarks and a held-out test set, while retrieval latency and index storage were measured to quantify operational cost. Performance patterns observed with small or controlled collections did not consistently persist as collections grew, and the usefulness of reranking depended on the corpus and retrieval setting. RAG improved three of four model configurations across the external benchmarks, with mean gains of up to 9.6 percentage points, and improved all four configurations on the held-out test set by 10.2-30.3 points. Abstract retrieval performed best when reference evidence was abstract-aligned, whereas full-text representations were generally more effective when richer evidence was needed. Hierarchical representation matched or outperformed flat full-text retrieval in most end-to-end comparisons while requiring 67% fewer indexed units and 44-56% less storage. These findings show that corpus scale should be treated as an explicit evaluation variable in biomedical RAG, and that the most appropriate design depends on evidence format, model behavior, and operational constraints.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for biomedical and medical
question answering, but answers based only on parametric knowledge may be
incomplete, outdated, or difficult to verify. Retrieval-Augmented Generation
(RAG) addresses this limitation by providing external documents at inference
time, allowing the generator to condition its answer on explicit evidence
rather than only on information encoded in its parameters [ 23 ] .

blocks.en:
The effectiveness of biomedical RAG depends not only on the generator, but also
on the retrieval corpus and on how its documents are represented. Expanding the
corpus may increase the availability of relevant evidence, but it also
introduces additional distractors and raises retrieval and storage costs.
Document representation creates a related trade-off. Abstracts are compact and
efficient, but may omit answer-relevant details. Full-text retrieval preserves
richer evidence, but substantially increases the number of indexed units and
may fragment information across independent chunks. Hierarchical
representations provide an alternative by retaining relationships between
different parts of a document.

These factors cannot be considered independently. As the source corpus grows,
each representation produces a retrieval index of a different size and
structure, which may affect first-stage retrieval, reranking, the evidence
provided to the generator, and ultimately the quality of the generated answer.
A representation that improves evidence coverage may therefore be impractical
because of its storage or latency requirements, while a reranker that improves
the final ranking may not necessarily improve downstream answer accuracy.

This study investigates these interactions through a controlled evaluation of
biomedical RAG systems under increasing corpus scale. We distinguish the number
of source documents from the representation-dependent number of retrievable
units and compare three document representations: abstracts, flat full-text
chunks, and TreeRAG-style hierarchical representations [ 42 ] . The experiments use PubMed as a large collection of real
biomedical literature and MIRIAD [ 52 ] as a controlled setting with
question-linked source passages.

blocks.en:
We evaluate the RAG pipeline both modularly and end-to-end. First-stage
retrieval and reranking are assessed separately to determine how corpus growth
affects evidence selection. Downstream performance is evaluated through
multiple-choice question answering (MCQA), using development datasets, external
biomedical benchmarks, and a held-out MIRIAD test split. We compare LLM-only and
RAG configurations across compact general-purpose, biomedical, and
reasoning-oriented generators, and use a dataset-specific Oracle condition to
characterize generation when reference evidence is directly available.
Retrieval latency and index storage are also measured to quantify the practical
cost of each configuration.

blocks.en:
To the best of our knowledge, existing biomedical RAG studies commonly evaluate
relatively small or task-specific retrieval collections, while a smaller number
use large indexes. However, these systems are generally assessed at a single
fixed corpus scale, and corpus growth is rarely analyzed jointly with document
representation, retrieval, reranking, downstream generation, and efficiency.
Consequently, it remains unclear whether conclusions obtained at one collection
size remain valid as biomedical knowledge resources grow. This study addresses
this gap through a controlled, system-level empirical evaluation of biomedical
RAG under corpus growth.

blocks.en:
Passage-level retrieval makes search over large collections tractable and
allows generators to use multiple evidence units [ 20 , 12 ] . However, fixed-size segmentation can
split relevant evidence, remove document-level context, and create redundant
units. Retrieval granularity therefore affects both retrieval and downstream
generation [ 26 , 3 ] .

instead seek to preserve broader document

into tree-structured retrieval units, enabling comparison between
abstract-level, flat full-text, and hierarchical
representations [ 42 ] .

MedAESQA and MIRIAD are originally formulated as open-ended QA tasks. We
convert them to MCQA while preserving the original reference answer as the
correct option and generating three incorrect distractors. The conversion
pipeline consists of three stages: generating medically plausible candidates,
rewriting them to reduce superficial cues such as differences in length or
syntax, and filtering and ranking the candidates to select the final
distractors. Correct-answer positions are balanced across option labels.
Implementation details, including model configuration, decoding parameters,
and filtering heuristics, are provided in Supplementary Section B.

blocks.en:
This section evaluates whether the retrieval-augmented pipeline selected during
development transfers beyond the datasets used for pipeline selection. We
consider two test settings. First, five external biomedical MCQA benchmarks
(MMLU-Med, MedQA-US, MedMCQA, PubMedQA, and BioASQ-Y/N) are evaluated using
the full PubMed corpus as the retrieval source. Second, the held-out
MIRIAD TEST split is evaluated using the large MIRIAD corpus. Although
MIRIAD TEST was not used for pipeline selection, it shares the same construction
process and corpus family as MIRIAD DEV and is therefore interpreted as an
in-domain held-out evaluation rather than as a fully external benchmark.

blocks.en:
Reranking introduces a substantial latency overhead for every first-stage
retriever. For BM25, reranking improves Recall@5 but moves the resulting
pipelines into the latency range of substantially more effective dense
retrieval configurations. Reranking BGE-base-en-v1.5 can further improve its
Recall@5, but only at a query-time cost that exceeds that of
Qwen3-Embedding-8B without reranking. For Qwen3-Embedding-8B, none of the
rerankers improves upon the first-stage Recall@5, and some reduce it while
increasing latency. Consequently, the three first-stage retrievers define the
observed latency–effectiveness frontier: Qwen3-Embedding-8B provides maximum
effectiveness, BGE-base-en-v1.5 offers a substantially lower-latency
alternative, and BM25 minimizes latency at the cost of lower recall.

blocks.en: 5 Discussion
blocks.zh: 5 讨论情况

blocks.en:
Our results show that biomedical RAG design choices should be evaluated in
relation to corpus scale. Larger retrieval pools broaden the available evidence
but also introduce additional distractors, making evidence selection more
difficult. The degradation observed for several retrieval configurations at the
largest corpus scales shows that conclusions obtained from small or controlled
collections do not necessarily transfer to large-scale biomedical retrieval.
Corpus scale should therefore be treated as an explicit evaluation variable and
considered jointly with document representation, retrieval quality, generator
behavior, and deployment cost.

The results also challenge the assumption that reranking is an inherently
beneficial stage. On MedAESQA, Qwen3-Embedding-8B obtains the strongest
Recall@5 without reranking, and the evaluated rerankers either preserve or
reduce effectiveness while increasing latency. On MIRIAD, reranking becomes
more useful as the retrieval pool grows, and Qwen3-Reranker-8B improves the
final evidence ranking at the largest scale. The utility of reranking therefore
depends on the quality of the first-stage ranking, the corpus, and the evidence
units being ranked. Its value should be established empirically rather than
assumed from improvements observed in smaller or different retrieval settings.

Finally, the efficiency analysis illustrates that the most effective
configuration is not necessarily the most practical one. Qwen3-Embedding-8B
provides the highest first-stage retrieval effectiveness but has substantially
higher latency than BGE-base-en-v1.5, while reranking introduces additional
cost without consistently improving Recall@5. Similarly, Full-text supports
strong downstream results but produces the largest indexes, whereas TreeRAG
retains competitive performance with a considerably smaller storage footprint.
The preferred biomedical RAG configuration therefore depends on the intended
deployment setting: maximum-effectiveness systems may justify larger models and
indexes, whereas latency- or storage-constrained applications may favor lighter
retrievers or more compact full-text representations.

blocks.en: 5.1 Limitations
blocks.zh: 5.1 限制

blocks.en:
This study has some limitations related to dataset scope and evaluation
design. MedAESQA contains relatively few questions, whereas MIRIAD provides a
larger but synthetically constructed setting. Moreover, MIRIAD TEST shares the
same construction process and corpus family as MIRIAD DEV and should therefore
be interpreted as an in-domain held-out evaluation. We complement these
controlled datasets with five independently constructed biomedical benchmarks
to assess transfer beyond the development settings.

与MIRIAD DEV相同的建筑过程和实体家庭,因此应当
被解释为域内搁置的评价。 我们补充这些
具有五个独立构建的生物医学基准的控制数据集
评估超出开发环境的转让。

blocks.en:
The evaluation is restricted to multiple-choice question answering, enabling
standardized comparisons across corpus scales, retrieval configurations, and
generators. It does not directly assess open-ended generation, explanation
quality, evidence citation, or clinical validity. In addition, retrieval is
evaluated through source-document matching because the gold evidence formats
differ across datasets and do not align exactly with all retrieval units.
Recall should therefore be interpreted as source-level evidence coverage
rather than exact evidence-unit matching.

blocks.en: 6 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 6 结论

blocks.en:
This work addresses an important limitation of existing biomedical RAG
evaluation: systems are commonly assessed at a single fixed corpus scale, even
when the retrieval index itself is large. Such evaluations cannot establish
whether an observed advantage remains robust as the collection grows. Under
controlled scaling across PubMed and MIRIAD, from the smallest conditions to
the full PubMed corpus and the complete MIRIAD collection, advantages observed
for retrievers, rerankers, and document representations at the control or tiny
scales did not consistently persist at larger scales, despite retaining the
available gold sources. Corpus scale should therefore be treated as an explicit
evaluation variable rather than assuming that results obtained at one
collection size will generalize to another.

No document representation was consistently optimal. Abstract retrieval was
effective when the reference evidence was abstract-aligned, whereas Full-text
and TreeRAG were generally stronger on the external benchmarks and MIRIAD.
TreeRAG provided a favorable effectiveness–efficiency trade-off, remaining
competitive with, and frequently outperforming, flat Full-text chunking while

characterization of biomedical RAG under corpus growth and operational
constraints. By jointly evaluating retrieval, reranking, generation, latency,
